title: CRLA/167/2013 of SMT VIJAY LAXMI Vs AJAY SINGH RANA

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No.167 of 2013
Smt. Vijay Laxmi Ö Appellant
Versus
Ajay Singh Rana Ö Respondent
Mr. N.S. Pundir, Advocate, for the appellant.
Mr. Sandeep Kothari, Advocate, for the respondent.
Honíble Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.
 Appellant/complainant Smt. Vijay Laxmi and the
accused/respondent Ajay Singh Rana are basically the
residents of District Tehri Garhwal. Some immovable land,
measuring 30 square meters, was allotted to the appellant by
the Tehri Dam Rehabilitation Authority. Appellant erected the
ground, first and second floors on that land. It appears that
the first and second floors erected upon that 30 square meters
land was covered with the total area of 186 (93+93) square
meters, as has been mentioned in the agreement to sale dated
15.07.2009. The respondent/accused purchased the same for
the actual total price of Rs.24.25 lakhs. This consideration
was paid by the accused/respondent to the appellant by way
of three post-dated cheques drawn by the respondent from his
banker. First Cheque dated 30.07.2009 was for the value of
Rs.7.00 lakhs; second Cheque dated 03.08.2009 was for the
value of Rs.11.00 lakhs whereas the third Cheque dated
30.10.2009 was worth Rs.6.25 lakhs.
 Unusually, the sale deed got executed just on the next
date i.e. 16.07.2009 but in order to avoid some stamp duty
and taxes, the total sale consideration was disclosed to be
Rs.11.00 lakhs. This sum was got by the appellant by way of
Cheque dated 03.08.2009. So, on an apparent look, the
transaction was, thus, completed. The fact remains that the
Cheque dated 30.07.2009, which was for the value of Rs.7.00
lakhs, was returned by the appellant to the purchaser Ajay

2
Singh Rana, and in lieu thereof, appellant received Rs.7.00
lakh in cash. This fact about receiving the cash and returning
that cheque was brought into writing.
 The dispute arose when the vendor/appellant asked
about Rs.6.25 lakhs in cash and the respondent, as he
claims, gave this amount to the appellant but the latter did
not return the Cheque dated 30.10.2009 to the purchaser.
Appellant has averred that in fact, this amount of Rs.6.25
lakhs was never given to her by the respondent. When, she
submitted this Cheque in the bank for encashment, it was
dishonoured on 04.11.2009, for the reason of insufficiency of
funds in the account of the respondent/purchaser.
 On 11.11.2009, the notice was issued to the
respondent, as envisaged under Section 138 of the Negotiable
Instruments Act (hereinafter will be referred to as ëthe Actí)
and the fact of receiving such notice is not in dispute.
 But, instead of receiving the notice, the envelope,
containing two blank papers, was accepted by the respondent.
The response was made on dated 20.11.2009.
 Respondent requested the appellant to deposit the
Cheque, in question, again in the Bank, and in the
meanwhile, he would manage the sufficiency of the funds in
his account. On such presentation, the said Cheque was
again dishonoured by the bank on 08.12.2009 but for a
different reason, i.e. the bank was asked to stop the payment.
 So, the bank returned the dishonoured Cheque to the
appellant on 15.12.2009. On 16.12.2009, she issued second
notice to the respondent, which was replied on 30.12.2009
with the averments that Rs.6.25 lakhs had already been given
to her in cash in front of one Mr. Uttam Singh, while she kept
on making the assurance for returning of the Cheque on one
pretext or the other, and ultimately returned the same, and it

3
is this Cheque, which is being misused by the appellant for
initiating the instant litigation under the Act.
 There is yet another aspect of this entire episode that the
appellant made a complaint to the Collector concerned to the
effect that the sale deed has been executed in far less price
than the Government rate prevailing in the area. So, the
notice was issued from the concerned Officer and the
valuation of the sold property was Rs.24.25 lakhs. Thus, the
remaining amount of the stamp duty, which was exigible on
the sale deed, was recovered from the respondent.
 Learned counsel for the respondent has based his
arguments that in any case, this sum of Rs.6.25 lakh, the
disputed amount, was not a legally enforceable debt or other
liability, as has been adumbrated under Section 138 of the
Act because the appellant cannot recover this amount by way
of filing a civil suit. So, this is not a legally enforceable debt.
 The Court is unable to agree with the said contention
because the truth is reflected from the language of the
agreement to sale executed between the parties on
15.07.2009, whereas the entire sale transaction was agreed to
be 24.25 lakhs, and this amount of Rs.6.25 lakhs was a part
of that total amount. The truth is that the property was sold
not for Rs.11 lakhs but was for Rs.24.25 lakhs. All the same,
the amount of Rs.11 lakhs was only a price, which was
displayed in the sale deed fictitiously, obviously, for the
reasons, as aforementioned. This fact gets strength from the
letter of the concerned revenue official asking the respondent
to deposit the remaining stamp duty, which he deposited.
 The contention of the respondent that this amount of
Rs.6.25 lakhs was paid to the appellant, in cash, in front of
one Mr. Uttam Singh, is unacceptable to this Court for the
reason that the cases under this Act do not require the strict
proof and it does not lay the onus of proving the allegations

4
entirely upon the complainant likewise a criminal case. It is a
semi-criminal and a semi-civil case in nature.
 When the defendant/accused has taken a defence, then
the burden shifts upon him to prove that fact. Likewise, if the
respondent has taken the plea that Rs.6.25 lakhs were paid in
front of Mr. Uttam Singh, then it was his bounden duty to get
that person examined as a witness, so that to render an
opportunity to the complainant also to cross-examine that
witness on this score.
 Otherwise also, it is beyond comprehension of a
common prudent man that the respondent paid such a
handsome amount, inasmuch as, to the tune of Rs.6.25 lakhs
and accepted the excuse of the appellant that the concerned
Cheque was kept in a bank-locker, which she would return
after sometime.
 So, in view of what has been stated above, I find
force in this appeal. It is hereby allowed. Impugned judgment
and order passed by the Trial Court is hereby set aside.
Respondent Ajay Singh Rana is found guilty for the offence of
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act wherefor he is
sentenced to six monthsí imprisonment with fine of
Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand Only).
 It is however, directed that in case, within eight weeks
from today, the respondent makes payment of Rs.6.25 lakhs
along with 9% compound interest per annum thereon, to the
appellant, calculating the period w.e.f. 30.10.2009, then the
sentence of imprisonment, as passed against him by this
Court, will be inoperative. But in that eventuality too, the
respondent shall deposit the fine of Rs. 50,000/- in the
Government Treasury, as ordered by this Court.
